extracted.intended_audience: judges, patent attorneys, law students, and practitioners analyzing patent infringement
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether an accused product or process infringes a patent, addressing process vs manufacture, principle/application identity, material differences, proportions, combinations, burden of proof, and utility/equivalency tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process versus manufacture rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the invention or subject-matter of the patent is a manufacture, it is immaterial by what process it is produced, since the infringement must consist in making the same thing; but where the invention is the process of making a particular thing, the inquiry is whether it has been made by the use of the process covered by the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If patent claims a manufacture, proof of making the same article can establish infringement even if produced by a different process, unless it appears the article could be produced by an independent process. If patent claims a process, plaintiff must show the defendant used that process. Examples: making the same article may suffice; but for process patents the identity of method is dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof on plaintiff
rubrics_metrics.description: The burthen of proof of the infringement is upon the plaintiff throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In absence of direct evidence of use of a patented process, similarity of the effect produced and evidence of use of similar apparatus will generally be sufficient to establish infringement. The plaintiff must persuade the jury the defendant used the patentee's process; otherwise verdict should favor defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the subject-matter/claim before testing infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The first thing to be attended to is the subject-matter of the patent; a clear idea is to be formed of the object of the patent, and provided the specification properly points out what the claim of the patentee is, it is not material in what form his claim is presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine what the specification and claims actually cover (principle, application, process, manufacture). The form (labeled process or manufacture) is subordinate to the real subject covered; infringement analysis proceeds from that identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial identity of principle and application
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the real subject covered by the patent is the application of a principle in the arts or manufactures, the question on an infringement will be as to the substantial identity of the principle and of the application of the principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means, machinery, forms or modifications are material only insofar as they affect the identity of the application. Cases (Forsyth, Clegg) show varied apparatus or constructions do not avoid infringement if the same principle is applied in substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material addition / distinct subject-matter test
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendants have added anything material not covered by the plaintiff's patent which could be considered as constituting a subject-matter distinct from that of the plaintiff, there may be no infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine whether the accused product/process contains material differences in materials, mode of combination, or operation such that it constitutes a new subject-matter (e.g., mechanical vs chemical processes; different proportions or combination). If differences are real and substantial, they may support independent patentability and negate infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colorable imitation versus substantive difference
rubrics_metrics.description: A circuitous variation that attains the same principle or result may still be an infringement; but a genuine, substantial difference (not a mere colorable device) may negate infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the alleged differences are merely attempts to evade an earlier patent (fraud on the patent) or real changes in materials/process producing a materially different effect or mode of operation. Walton v. Potter illustrates circuitous modes that still infringe; defendants' proof of mechanical vs chemical distinction can defeat infringement if substantial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportions/degrees as part of the essence of some patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Where proportions or degrees are specified as the mode in which a particular effect is to be produced, they make part of the essence of the invention, and departures in proportions may lead to a different subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent claims a combination that depends on particular proportions, use of the same ingredients in materially different proportions (even if producing a similar effect) can be a new invention and not an infringement. Courts will consider whether the specification treated those proportions as essential; slight departures intended only to evade are treated as fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slight departures for evasion are fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: A slight departure from the specification for the purpose of evasion only would be a fraud upon the patent and will not avoid infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing differences, courts look for substantive, not cosmetic, departures. Evidence that changes were made purely to evade existing claims supports finding of infringement; the test is whether the defendant's operation is essentially or substantially different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superior utility / practical difference test
rubrics_metrics.description: Two things are not the same under the patent law when one is practically, substantially better than the other, and this improvement is not gained by the use of known mechanical equivalents; superior utility may settle the question of identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If accused device achieves materially better practical results by means that are in fact different (not mere equivalents), it may be considered not the same under the law. Courts use this to limit overbroad claims to allow useful improvements to be separately patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination patent rule (using parts of a combination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent stands upon its subject-matter; where the patent is for a combination, it is no infringement to use any of the parts or things which go to make up the combination if the combination itself is not used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim is to an entire combination, merely practicing individual elements does not infringe unless the claimed combination (all essential elements) is practiced. Contrast with patents that claim several distinct improvements (below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct improvements rule (single-element infringement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patent is for several distinct improvements or things, and does not stand upon the combination of such things, then the use of any one of them will be an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a patent claims multiple separate inventions rather than a unitary combination, defendants using any one claimed improvement may infringe. Historically, courts required novelty of all claimed improvements to sustain an action; practitioners should be aware of that rule's significance in claim drafting and litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known mechanical equivalents doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Means that are in point of fact known mechanical equivalents may be treated as the same for purposes of infringement analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the accused device uses different structure, if that structure is a known equivalent that performs the same function in substantially the same way to achieve the same result, courts may find infringement. Evaluate whether the differences are mere known equivalents or true substantive changes.
